card.summary_ko: 《삼국사기》 설총전에 실린 우화로, 설총이 신문왕에게 화왕(꽃의 왕)과 장미·백두옹의 이야기를 들려 주며 임금이 아첨하는 이를 멀리해야 함을 일깨웁니다.
card.summary_en: A fable from the Samguk sagi biography of Seol Chong, in which he tells King Sinmun of the Flower King, the Rose and the White-headed Old Man to warn a ruler against flatterers.
card.edition_ko: 위키문헌(중문) 〈三國史記/卷46〉(薛聰 조), 판 2284357, CC BY-SA 4.0 (원저작물은 공유저작물)

notes.ko:
**저자** 이 글은 《삼국사기》(1145)에 실린 설총 열전 속의 우화로, 기록자는 김부식(1075–1151)입니다. 김부식은 경주 김씨 출신의 고려 문신으로 인종의 명을 받아 《삼국사기》를 편찬했고, 1135–36년 묘청의 난을 진압한 총사령관으로 개경 문벌 귀족과 유교적 보수 질서를 대표하는 인물입니다. 신채호 등 후대 민족주의 사학자는 그를 사대주의적이라고 비판했으나, 이는 평가가 갈리는 부분입니다. 우화의 화자 설총은 신라 신문왕(재위 681–692) 때의 유학자로, 원효의 아들이라고 전합니다.

**시대적 맥락** 신문왕은 즉위 직후 김흠돌의 반란(681)을 진압하고 귀족 세력을 누르며 왕권을 강화했고, 국학(682)을 세워 유학 교육을 장려했습니다. 이 이야기는 그런 분위기에서 왕이 신하에게 ‘이색적인 이야기’를 청하자 설총이 들려 준 것으로 전해지며, 이후 간언 문학의 고전으로 읽혔습니다.

**배경** 《삼국사기》 권46 열전 제6 ‘설총’ 조에 실려 있습니다. 설총 자신의 글은 전하지 않으므로, 이 우화가 실제 설총의 말인지, 어느 정도 김부식의 손을 거쳤는지는 확정할 수 없습니다. 모란(花王)을 임금으로 보는 해석은 후대의 것입니다. 이 본문에는 우화에 이어 설총의 간략한 전기가 함께 붙어 있습니다.

**의의** 한국 최초의 우화적 창작물로 자주 소개되며, 의인화 수법은 고려 가전체(임춘 〈국순전〉, 이규보 〈국선생전〉)와 조선 후기 우화소설에 이어졌습니다. 또한 충신과 간신, 가까이할 사람과 멀리할 사람에 대한 유교적 군주 교육의 교재 구실을 했습니다.

**형식과 주제** 한문 산문의 틀 안에 4자·6자 대구(‘當三春而發艶，凌百花而獨出’)를 쓴 변려문풍 문체가 보입니다. 장미(미인, 아첨)와 백두옹(할미꽃, 쓴 약처럼 쓸모 있는 충신)의 대비를 통해, 달콤한 말을 하는 이를 가까이하지 말고 쓴소리를 하는 이를 가려 쓰라는 교훈을 담고 있습니다. 장부의 말 가운데 맹가(맹자)와 풍당의 사례는 훌륭한 인물이 불우했던 고사입니다.

**읽기 도움**
- 桑門(상문): 승려 / 小性居士: 설총이 승복을 벗은 뒤의 호
- 方言(방언): 여기서는 신라의 말, 즉 우리말로 경전을 풀이했다는 뜻
- 薦枕(천침): 베개를 올림, 곧 잠자리를 모심
- 膏梁(고량): 기름진 음식 / 惡石(악석): 병을 고치는 돌침
- 絲麻 / 菅蒯: 비단·삼과 띠·골풀 — 귀한 것이 있어도 천한 것을 버리지 말라
- 邪倿(사녕): 간사하고 아첨하는 사람
- 愀然(초연): 얼굴빛을 고쳐 정색하는 모양
- 追贈(추증): 죽은 뒤 관직·시호를 내림 / 弘儒侯: 설총에게 내린 봉호
notes.en:
**About the author** The fable comes from the biography of Seol Chong in the Samguk sagi (1145), recorded by Kim Bu-sik (1075–1151). Kim, from the Gyeongju Kim family, was a Goryeo civil official who compiled the work on the order of King Injong and, as commander, crushed the monk Myocheong’s rebellion in 1135–36; he stands for the Gaegyeong aristocracy and the conservative Confucian order. Later nationalist historians such as Sin Chaeho criticised him as deferring to China, a verdict that remains contested. The narrator, Seol Chong, was a Confucian scholar under King Sinmun of Silla (r. 681–692), traditionally the son of the monk Wonhyo.

**Historical context** Sinmun began his reign by crushing Kim Heum-dol’s rebellion (681), curbed noble power, strengthened the throne, and in 682 founded the National Academy (Gukhak) to promote Confucian education. The story is said to come from this atmosphere: the king asked his subject for an unusual tale, and Seol Chong answered with the fable. It was long read as a classic of remonstrance.

**Background** It appears in Samguk sagi, vol. 46, biography no. 6, “Seol Chong.” None of Seol Chong’s own writings survive, so it cannot be established how far the fable reproduces his words or how much passed through Kim Bu-sik’s hands. Identifying the Flower King with the peony is a later reading. The passage here also includes a short biography of Seol Chong after the fable.

**Significance** It is often introduced as the earliest fable in Korean literature; its personification technique runs through the Goryeo gajeon (biographies of objects, e.g. Im Chun’s and Yi Gyu-bo’s) and the later Joseon animal fables. It also served as Confucian teaching material on whom a ruler should keep near and whom at a distance.

**Form and themes** Within classical Chinese prose, it uses paired four- and six-character phrases in a parallel-prose manner (當三春而發艷，凌百花而獨出). The contrast between the Rose (beauty, flattery) and the White-headed Old Man (the pasqueflower, a bitter-but-useful remedy, i.e. the loyal remonstrator) teaches the king not to favour sweet talkers but to choose those who speak harshly. The old man’s examples of Mencius and Feng Tang are well-known stories of worthy men left unrewarded.

**Reading help**
- 桑門 (sangmun): Buddhist monk; 小性居士: the name Seol Chong took after leaving the robe
- 方言 (bangeon): here the Silla vernacular, i.e. explaining the classics in the native tongue
- 薦枕 (cheonchim): ‘offer the pillow’, i.e. to share the bed
- 膏梁 (gollyang): rich food; 惡石 (agseok): a stone lancet used in medicine
- 絲麻 / 菅蒯: silk and hemp / rushes and reeds — do not discard the humble when you have the precious
- 邪倦 (saryeong): crooked flatterers
- 愁然 (choyeon): to change countenance gravely
- 追贈 (chuzeung): posthumous grant of rank or title; 弘儒侯: Marquis Hongyu

paragraphs.orig: 薛聰，字聰智。祖談捺奈麻，父元曉。初爲桑門，掩該佛書，旣而返本，自號小性居士。聰性明銳，生知道，待以方言，讀《九經》，訓導後生，至今學者宗之。又能屬文，而世無傳者。但今南地或有聰所製碑銘，文字鈌落不可讀，竟不知其何如也。神文大王以仲夏之月，處高明之室，顧謂聰曰：「今日宿雨初歇，薰風微凉，雖有珍饌哀音，不如高談善謔，以舒伊鬱。吾子必有異聞，盍爲我陳之？」聰曰：「唯。臣聞昔花王之始來也，植之以香園，護之以翠幕，當三春而發艶，凌百花而獨出。於是自邇及遐，艶艶之靈，夭夭之英，無不奔走上謁，唯恐不及。忽有一佳人，朱顔玉齒，鮮粧靚服，伶俜而來，綽約而前曰：『妾履雪白之沙汀，對鏡淸之海而，沐春雨以去垢，快淸風而自適，其名曰薔薇。聞王之令德，期薦枕於香帷，王其容我乎？』又有一丈夫，布衣韋帶，戴白持杖，龍鍾而步，傴僂而來，曰：『僕在京城之外，居大道之旁，下臨蒼茫之野景，上倚嵯峨之山色，其名曰白頭翁。竊謂左右供給雖足，膏梁以充腸，茶酒以淸神，巾衍儲藏，須有良藥以補氣，惡石以蠲毒。故曰雖有絲麻，無棄菅蒯。凡百君子，無不代匱。不識王亦有意乎？』或曰：『二者之來，何取何捨？』花王曰：『丈夫之言，亦有道理，而佳人難得，將如之何？』丈夫進而言曰：『吾謂王聰明識理義，故來焉耳，今則非也。凡爲君者，鮮不親近邪倿，疎遠正直。是以孟軻不遇以終身，馮唐郞潛而皓首。自古如此，吾其奈何？』花王曰：『吾過矣，吾過矣！』」於是王愀然作色曰：「子之寓言，誠有深志。請書之，以謂王者之戒。」遂擢聰以高秩。世傳日本國眞人贈新羅使薛判官詩序云：「嘗覽元曉居士所著《金剛三昧論》，深恨不見其人。聞新羅國使薛，卽是居士之抱孫，雖不見其祖，而喜遇其孫，乃作詩贈之。」其詩至今存焉，但不知其子孫名字耳。至我顯宗，在位十三歲，天禧五年辛酉，追贈爲弘儒侯。或云薛聰嘗入唐學，未知然不？
paragraphs.reading: 설총, 자총지. 조담날나마, 부원효. 초위상문, 엄해불서, 기이반본, 자호소성거사. 총성명예, 생지도, 대이방언, 독《구경》, 훈도후생, 지금학자종지. 우능촉문, 이세무전자. 단금남지혹유총소제비명, 문자결락불가독, 경부지기하여야. 신문대왕이중하지월, 처고명지실, 고위총왈: 「금일숙우초헐, 훈풍미량, 수유진찬애음, 불여고담선학, 이서이울. 오자필유이문, 합위아진지?」 총왈: 「유. 신문석화왕지시래야, 식지이향원, 호지이취막, 당삼춘이발염, 능백화이독출. 어시자이급하, 염염지령, 요요지영, 무불분주상알, 유공불급. 홀유일가인, 주안옥치, 선장정복, 영빙이래, 작약이전왈: 『첩리설백지사정, 대경청지해이, 목춘우이거구, 쾌청풍이자적, 기명왈장미. 문왕지령덕, 기천침어향유, 왕기용아호?』 우유일장부, 포의위대, 대백지장, 용종이보, 구루이래, 왈: 『복재경성지외, 거대도지방, 하림창망지야경, 상의차아지산색, 기명왈백두옹. 절위좌우공급수족, 고량이충장, 다주이청신, 건연저장, 수유양약이보기, 악석이견독. 고왈수유사마, 무기관괴. 범백군자, 무불대궤. 불식왕역유의호?』 혹왈: 『이자지래, 하취하사?』 화왕왈: 『장부지언, 역유도리, 이가인난득, 장여지하?』 장부진이언왈: 『오위왕총명식이의, 고래언이, 금즉비야. 범위군자, 선불친근사녕, 소원정직. 시이맹가불우이종신, 풍당랑잠이호수. 자고여차, 오기내하?』 화왕왈: 『오과의, 오과의!』」 어시왕초연작색왈: 「자지우언, 성유심지. 청서지, 이위왕자지계.」 수탁총이고질. 세전일본국진인증신라사설판관시서운: 「상람원효거사소저《금강삼매론》, 심한불견기인. 문신라국사설, 즉시거사지포손, 수불견기조, 이희우기손, 내작시증지.」 기시지금존언, 단부지기자손명자이. 지아현종, 재위십삼세, 천희오년신유, 추증위홍유후. 혹운설총상입당학, 미지연부?
paragraphs.en: Seol Chong, courtesy name Chongji. His grandfather was Damnal, of the Naema rank; his father was Wonhyo. At first he became a Buddhist monk and mastered the Buddhist scriptures; later he returned to lay life and called himself Layman Soseong. Chong was by nature quick and keen and knew the Way from birth; using the vernacular he read the Nine Classics and instructed the young, and to this day scholars take him as their master. He could also compose literary writings, but none survive in the world. Only in the southern region there may be inscriptions made by Chong, but the characters are broken and cannot be read, so in the end it is not known what they were like. King Sinmun, in the midsummer month, seated in a high and bright chamber, turned to Chong and said: “Today the long rain has just cleared and the warm breeze is faintly cool. Though there are fine dishes and sad music, they are no match for lofty talk and good jesting to ease this gloom. You must have some unusual tale; why not tell it to me?” Chong said: “Yes. I have heard that long ago, when the Flower King first came, he was planted in a fragrant garden and sheltered with kingfisher-green curtains; in the three months of spring he bloomed in splendour and rose alone above the hundred flowers. Then, from near and far, the spirits of beauty and the blossoms of loveliness all hurried to pay their respects, fearing only to be too late. Suddenly there was a beautiful woman, with rosy face and teeth like jade, in bright make-up and fine clothes, who came alone and drew near gracefully, saying: ‘I have walked the white sands of the shore, faced the sea clear as a mirror, bathed in spring rain to wash away the dust and delighted in the pure breeze, content in myself; my name is Rose. Hearing of your Majesty’s virtue, I hope to offer my pillow in your fragrant curtains. Will the King accept me?’ Then there was also a man, in cloth garments and a leather belt, white-capped and holding a staff, who walked tottering and came bent over, and said: ‘I live outside the capital, beside the great road; below me lies the vast expanse of open fields, and above me the lofty mountains. My name is White-headed Old Man. I think that although those around you supply you well—rich food to fill the belly, tea and wine to refresh the spirit, and your cabinets and cases stocked—you must also have good medicine to restore the vital breath and sharp stones to drive out poison. Therefore it is said: though you have silk and hemp, do not throw away rushes and reeds. All gentlemen, without exception, need something to make up for what is lacking. I do not know whether the King too has a mind for this.’ Someone said: ‘Of the two who have come, which will you take and which leave?’ The Flower King said: ‘The man’s words too have reason, but a beautiful woman is hard to find. What shall I do?’ The man stepped forward and said: ‘I thought the King was wise and understood principle and righteousness, and so I came; but now it is not so. Of all who are rulers, few do not draw near to the crooked and flattering and keep far from the upright. That is why Mencius went unrecognised to the end of his life, and Feng Tang remained a lowly official until his hair was white. It has been so since antiquity; what can I do?’ The Flower King said: ‘I was wrong, I was wrong!’” Thereupon the King changed countenance gravely and said: “Your fable truly holds a deep meaning. Please write it down, so that it may serve as a warning to kings.” He then promoted Chong to a high rank. It is handed down that in the preface to a poem presented to the Silla envoy, Assistant Official Seol, by a Japanese ‘true man’ (Mahito), it says: “I once read the Geumgang sammae non written by the Layman Wonhyo and deeply regretted not meeting its author. I heard that the Silla envoy Seol is this layman’s grandson; though I could not see the grandfather, I am glad to meet the grandson, and so I have written this poem to present to him.” The poem survives to this day, but the names of his descendants are not known. In the reign of our Hyeonjong, in the thirteenth year of his rule, the fifth year of Tianxi, the year sinyu, he was posthumously granted the title Marquis Hongyu. Some say that Seol Chong once went to Tang to study, but it is not known whether this is so.
